transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I’ve completely lost interest in the design work and hobbies that usually keep me grounded, and I can’t seem to care about anything right now. It’s just really hard to get through the day when everything feels so completely pointless.

Have you had other periods in the past when you felt depressed and lost interest like this for at least two weeks, or is this the first time it has happened? Was this brought on by a specific stressful event or major life change?

These cycles of crashing into heavy lows have been happening off and on for about a year, with this current deep low dragging on for close to a year and getting much worse over the past month. It really ramped up when my spouse and I separated, which happened right around the same time my workload at the design firm became incredibly demanding.

During this worst period, have you had any hallucinations or strong false beliefs that others said weren’t true, or has it been severe but without anything like that? Also, have you still been able to work and manage basic daily tasks, or has it become nearly impossible?

No, I haven't had any hallucinations or beliefs like that, but managing my daily life and work has become nearly impossible. I've missed multiple client deadlines, stopped showing up to teach my community classes, and let basic chores like laundry, cooking, and emails slide so much that both my boss and sister have intervened.

Before this current long low started, was there ever a separate period of at least two weeks when you felt similarly depressed or lost interest, and then mostly returned to your usual self in between? Or has this been one continuous episode tied to the separation and work stress?

This current deep low has been dragging on for close to a year, getting especially severe over the past month. But it hasn't been one continuous flat line; instead, I've gone through cycles of feeling overly revved up and energized before crashing back down into these heavy lows, which really ramped up around the time of my separation.

During those overly revved-up periods, did you ever have psychotic symptoms like hearing or seeing things others couldn’t, or strongly held beliefs that others said weren’t true? Also, did those periods ever require hospitalization or cause such severe impairment that you couldn’t function safely?

No, I never had any hallucinations or false beliefs during those high times, and I've never been hospitalized or unable to function safely. I was actually extremely active and on the go, though I did make some impulsive decisions like booking an expensive solo trip and putting money into a friend's sketchy startup.

During those energized periods, did they last at least a week and include things like needing much less sleep, talking much more, racing thoughts, or feeling unusually grand or unstoppable? Or were they shorter and milder, more like a noticeable boost in energy without that level of intensity?

They usually lasted for a couple of weeks, and during that time I only slept three or four hours a night but woke up feeling totally sharp and energized. I felt completely unstoppable, like I had an endless motor running to reorganize my apartment at 2 a.m. and take on massive workloads, though I got pretty snappy if anyone tried to slow me down.

opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes bipolar mood episodes with distinct hypomanic periods lasting a couple of weeks, featuring decreased need for sleep, increased energy/activity, irritability, impulsive spending/investment, and grandiose/unstoppable feelings, followed by a current severe depressive episode with marked anhedonia and major functional impairment. There is no evidence of psychotic symptoms during either pole and no history of hospitalization or mania severe enough to indicate a manic episode, supporting bipolar affective disorder, current episode mild or moderate depression (F31.3) rather than a depressive disorder alone.
